chunks: Concerns about brushes. The question: What are some concerns about brushes?
Brushes cause four kinds of trouble. They wear out, because they rub on a moving surface. They lose some voltage and make electrical noise.
They create friction and sometimes squeal. And their dust and sparks can cause problems in some environments.
These are the reasons designers sometimes choose brushless motors instead.
Think of the brake pads on a bicycle. They grip a spinning rim, so they slowly wear away, make dust, and sometimes squeal.
Brushes rub on the commutator in much the same way, and every bit of wear shortens the motor's life.
The analogy has one gap: brushes also carry current, so sparking and voltage drop come on top of the mechanical wear.
The reactance voltage rises linearly with speed because the commutation time shrinks.
At 6000 rpm it is a small fraction of the brush drop; near 30,000 rpm it is comparable, so commutation worsens, sparks appear and the brush grade and position become critical.
(A simplified model: real commutation depends on the brush width, the resistance of the film and the field in the neutral zone.)
Brush wear: the slow loss of brush material from rubbing and sparking. Contact voltage drop: the voltage lost where a brush touches the commutator, roughly 0.
5–1 volts per carbon brush. Arcing: small sparks at the contact. Commutator: the ring of copper segments on the spinning shaft that the brushes rub on.
Spring pressure: the force pushing the brush onto the commutator. Brushless motor: a motor with no sliding contacts.
Suppose a motor's brushes last 2,000 hours, and the motor runs 8 hours a day. That gives 2,000 / 8 = 250 days, so less than a year before the brushes need attention.
If the product must last years, you either change the brushes, derate the motor (lower speed or current), or switch to a brushless motor.
That is the whole idea: every brush concern comes from a sliding, sparking contact.
"The concerns are wear and finite life, electrical drop and loss, arcing noise, and speed and current limits. Brushes wear and make dust, typically thousands of hours.
They drop about a volt each, which matters at low voltage. Commutation of an inductive coil causes sparks and EMI.
Too much current density overheats them, and at high speed they bounce. Humidity, altitude and contamination change their behaviour and sparks are an ignition risk.
So pick the grade, suppress noise, derate, or go brushless."
